topic: The Ben Franklin effect: does asking for a favor make people like you?
title: Does Asking for a Favor Make People Like You?
voiceover: Does asking someone for a favor make them like you? In 1969, researchers Jecker and Landy invited students to a quiz competition where they could win money. Afterward, one group was asked by the researcher to return the money, because he'd used his own funds. Another group was asked by a secretary, citing department funds. A third group was not asked at all. Students the researcher himself had asked reported liking him more than students asked by the secretary. The classic explanation is cognitive dissonance: if you helped someone, you may conclude you must like them. It's one 1969 experiment, so treat the result as a suggestion, not a rule. So if you want to build rapport, asking for a small favor may help, but it's not guaranteed. Tomorrow: can you spot a liar from their body language?

In a 1969 experiment, students the researcher personally asked for money back reported liking him more than students asked by a secretary. New psychology short every day on The Psyche Discourse. Source: Jecker, J., & Landy, D. (1969). Liking a person as a function of doing him a favour. Human Relations, 22(4), 371-378.
accuracy_note: One classic 1969 experiment, known to us through several consistent summaries rather than the original paper. Cognitive dissonance is the classic explanation, not a proven mechanism. The 'small favor may help' takeaway is an application of the finding, not a tested tip.
